title: Dollarization remains a risk for Uruguay
text:
LUIS CUSTODIO Uruguayan economist Javier Bianchi - Senior Researcher at the Federal Reserve of Minnneapolis (*) - along with a student at the University of Minnesota, Jorge Mondragón, recently developed research that shows that the inability to use monetary policy for macroeconomic stabilization leaves to a government more vulnerable to a liquidity crisis. "A government with monetary autonomy can stabilize the economy and can easily remain immune to a maturity crisis," explains Bianchi. He understands that these risks are also present in dollarized economies such as Uruguay. He believes that greater management of macroprudential regulation puts countries like ours less exposed to this type of problem. Coming up a summary of the interview.

 - Did the lack of monetary autonomy play a key role in the last major crisis in Europe?>> - We highlighted the importance of monetary policy to determine how exposed a government is to a roll over crisis; Many of the works carried out in this area were previously motivated in Mexico, which had a debt of 270 days, but today European countries have a maturity in their debt of 5 to 7 years, so the result is that if these economies If they were in a position to use their monetary policy, they would be quite immune to a roll-over crisis, but because they are tied to EU policies, they are very exposed. When there is a recession, you can not count on this monetary policy tool. In this context, investors anticipate that if the government pays the debt that will have a recessive effect so the government will be more costly to pay the debt. Therefore, they are more prone to "run" when they perceive that other investors are not willing to lend to the government. They generate something like a bank run, but for governments.>> - You tested your theory with data from Spain from 1996 to 2015 ...>> - The case of Spain is interesting because it has had very high levels of unemployment and a very strong recession, and the spreads at the time were at levels of 500 basis points. If one compares it with other countries like England, despite having higher debt levels, it had clearly lower SpreadS. According to our study, that would be a product of the independence of the monetary policy of England, unlike Spain. - What lessons does this process leave?>> - What suggests for the framework of the European Union is that there should be an institutional policy of the European Central Bank to somehow act as a lender of last resort in such situations. In a way he did it, spontaneously and informally, when Mario Draghi said he would do whatever it took to preserve the Euro. The ECB president said it and had an impact on the market, but at the time there was a lot of resistance, particularly from Germany, so it was not clear to what extent the ECB was going to rescue these countries, which generated a lot of uncertainty. That is why we understand that this should be more institutionalized and not be left to political push. >> - What result would arise from applying in Uruguay the logic used in that study?>> - In Uruguay we have a flexible exchange rate. Even so, there are limitations to the activity of monetary policy, particularly because the Uruguayan economy is highly dollarized. So, that monetary policy instrument has limitations. In the future, if a government wants to devalue to alleviate a recession, problems will arise due to the dollarization of bank liabilities. Basically, this is a lesson that applies not only to countries that have a fixed exchange rate or to a monetary union, but also to countries with flexible exchange rates.but in which there are limitations as is clearly ours. - What should be done in the hypothesis of facing a situation like the one described? >> - In this scenario the government should resort to raising taxes a lot or to control spending drastically, and that would generate recessive events, which would make even more difficult the payment of the debt. To get rid of this situation requires a strategy of de-dollarization of the economy; This is a topic that has been talked about for a long time, a lesson we learned in the 2002 crisis. Efforts have been made to reduce this dollarization, particularly public debt, but if you look at bank deposits they are still highly denominated in dollars and part of the credits too. Changing that requires a longer-term monetary program than usual. >> When you have a fairly high inflation for international standards such as Uruguay, that inflation tends to be more volatile. That does not help to de-dollarize because people do not want to be exposed to the risks of the exchange rate. It has been difficult to achieve a more controlled inflation that remains within the established ranges and that does not help to lower dollarization levels.>> The other way to deal with this situation is through a macroprudential policy. The problem is that banks do not internalize that when they are anchored in dollars they make the whole system more unstable. Private motives are not aligned with social benefits, which is why government intervention and Central Bank regulation are needed. One can not tell the banks to operate with this or that currency, you have to give them incentives to do so. That's where the possibility of intervening happens. - What is your reading about macroprudential management in Uruguay?>> - I understand that Uruguay could resort more to macroprudential regulation. Immediately after the crisis of 2002 it seemed that the lesson was very clear. At that time I worked at the Central Bank and discussed the need to establish different capital requirements for the case of pesos or dollars, reserve requirements, and insisted a lot on those policies aimed at discouraging loans and deposits from being Dollars. My impression is that the use of these policies has not been sufficiently specified and that we are a little far from applying these policies compared to other countries. For example, in Peru, the reserve requirement for a deposit is 5% if it is in pesos and 35% if it is in dollars. In Uruguay meanwhile, the difference between the two currencies is only 6%. The BCU has a great capacity to use its influence to try to soften the financial cycle. Today a very strong consumption boom has been generated that has allowed higher welfare levels, but this also contributes to having more inflation, greater real appreciation of the currency and since salaries are quite rigid downwards, these are factors of vulnerability . - The best tool is a fiscal rule?>> - The fiscal rules help a lot, and the example of Chile is a good case to follow. It is a fact that governments in turn always want to spend more than what is optimal for society, therefore a political agreement is needed to limit future spending. You have to adjust the accounts for the product and for the cycle, that's clear, then, there are different criteria to apply. They are all valid; we must look for the one in which the political agreement is reached. >> - The last monetary decision of the Fed was surrounded by great financial volatility; What will happen to the United States?>> - Clearly there is uncertainty about how quickly the normalization process will take place. It is worrying that, by trying to keep inflation no higher than 2%, an increase in theeconomy. Nor is it known what the neutral level of the interest rate is. In this context, what is done is a risk examination. What would happen if the rate is raised to a certain level or not raised? And what is the true risk that exists. That is something that is done regularly by the Federal Reserve. And then comes the decision, which is based on what matters most, sticking to a pattern of inflation or allowing further expansion of the economy. In the Fed there are many who understand that if you let go a little inflation will be very difficult to achieve "bring" back. Therefore, they are very cautious, although inflation expectations are very anchored in society, and that is a very important value. Today in the Fed there seems to be very divided positions regarding the strategy to follow with respect to rates.>> - How much do Trump's public statements affect the decisions of the Fed?>> - In historical terms, it is unusual for the President be publicly expressed about the decisions of the Federal Reserve. I am in the Fed and there are no political issues discussed at all. The Federal Reserve is completely independent, which is a very strong institutional value that must be preserved.>> (*) Your opinions are personal and do not represent the Federal Reserve of Minneapolis or the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve. >

title: Moody's doubts that Argentina crisis contagion to Latin America
text:
It is unlikely that the turmoil in Argentina's financial markets will spread to the rest of Latin America, except possibly Uruguay, an analyst at rating agency Moody's said on Tuesday. A weak economic context, the nervousness with respect to the devaluation and the preoccupation by the crop of soybean hit by the drought in Argentina are pressing to the Argentine peso, that this week fell to a historical minimum against the dollar. Lee: Argentine President faces judicial process of course money laundering. "It is difficult to see a contagion of Argentina's agitation in Latin America," said Mauro Leos, head of sovereign risk at the agency for Latin America and the Caribbean at a conference in London, adding the possible exception in Uruguay. Lee: The central bank of Argentina performs a strong intervention in the foreign exchange market.

 The country is facing a crisis and on Tuesday the sovereign bonds in the over-the-counter market of Argentina fall 0.9% on average, in times of currency tension in the domestic market and a rapprochement of the Government to the IMF to negotiate a line of credit. The declining trend in government securities was led by dollar-denominated issues, operators said.

title: DJ UPDATE: Uruguay 'Isn't Prepared' to Sacrifice Growth to Trim Inflation -  Central Bank  Chief
text:
(Adds background on capital flow restrictions.) 


 
   By Ken Parks 
 

MONTEVIDEO, Uruguay--Uruguay "isn't prepared" to sacrifice economic growth in order to lower the inflation rate, the country's central bank president said in an interview.

Inflation stood at 8.14% in April, outside the central bank's target range of 4% to 6%. The central bank has fought rising prices by setting some of the region's highest interest rates and requiring banks to hold more cash. But it hasn't raised its main policy rate since December, when it increased it to 9.25%.

Central Bank President Mario Bergara said authorities have preferred policies to gradually slow inflation instead of taking more drastic measures that might harm the economy.

"Everybody understands that to make an effort to lower inflation about two points could mean an impact on growth, employment and above all social indicators like poverty, indigence and equality," Mr. Bergara said. "Uruguayan society isn't prepared to do that."

Uruguay's economy expanded by nearly 4% in 2012, and is expected to expand at about the same rate this year. But that is slower than in the previous few years. Also, Uruguayans still recall the state of the economy following Argentina's financial crisis in 2001, when trade shriveled and Uruguay's banks went bust. Thousands of Uruguayans were forced to seek work in other Latin American countries and in Europe.

Today, a tight labor market and high global commodity prices have stoked inflation, Mr. Bergara said. The central bank is also battling a strengthening Uruguayan peso.

"This year the problem of capital inflows has flared up with respect to prior years," Mr. Bergara said. "In the past two years market interventions were relatively low, and this year they have increased."

Uruguay's currency and bonds have become popular with foreign investors due to the country's high interest rates.

The Uruguayan peso has appreciated 1.1% against the dollar this year and nearly 15% since July. It traded Monday at UYU18.97 to the greenback. The peso's rise has sparked concerns that the currency's strength will make exports uncompetitive and stifle economic growth.

"The central bank and the government are supporting the exchange rate because if we didn't intervene, it would be much lower than where it is [now]," Mr. Bergara said.

Uruguay's central bank doesn't have a target exchange rate. It appears to be an active buyer of dollars in the currency market, with its international reserves rising $611 million this year to $14.2 billion.

Investors like Uruguay's bonds for their high yield and the steady peso, which has largely avoided the volatility that has struck other Latin American currencies this year, said Siobhan Morden, head of Latin American strategy at Jefferies.

The upward pressure on the peso will likely persist until interest rates in developed countries start to rise, Mr. Bergara said.

Latin American countries such as Brazil, Colombia and Chile have tried with varying degrees of success to dissuade speculative investments through capital controls, dollar purchases and other measures.

Uruguay began in October to require foreign investors who buy central bank notes to deposit 40% of the value of those securities in a special account to make that trade less profitable.

Mr. Bergara said that measure has been successful, though foreign investors have piled into government bonds and central bank notes traded on the secondary market

Authorities are constantly monitoring capital flows, said Mr. Bergara, who declined to comment on whether further "capital flow management" policies might be adopted.

Frequent interventions have left Uruguay with a war chest of foreign reserves equal to about 28% of gross domestic product.

Mr. Bergara described the reserves as an insurance policy for when the cycle turns, and investors start pulling their money from the country.

The central bank plans as early as this year to invest a portion of its reserves in higher-yielding securities, such as those of emerging markets in Asia.

"We have so much in reserves that we can create a portfolio where we can relax liquidity and credit rating requirements a little bit...to see if we can get a little bit more profitability," Mr. Bergara said.

-Prabha Natarajan contributed to this article.

title: MOODY'S LOWERS FOREIGN  CURRENCY  DEPOSIT AND DEBT RATINGS OF BANCO COMERCIAL S.A. AND BANCO DE MONTEVIDEO S.A.
text:
Moody's Investors Service 

 Moody's Investors Service downgraded to Ca from Caa1 the long term foreign currency ratings of both Banco Comercial S.A. (Comercial) and Banco de Montevideo S.A. (Montevideo), Uruguay's two largest domestically owned private sector banks. 

 Moody's lowered the long term deposit, and senior and subordinated debt ratings of Comercial and the long term deposit and senior debt ratings of Montevideo in light of indications by the Central Bank of Uruguay that it would only cover the demand deposit and savings account obligations of those privately-owned banks whose operations have been suspended. The implication is that the long term fixed rate deposits in US dollars held at those banks as well as their debt obligations would therefore be subject to the banks' own ability to meet those obligations. 

 Moody's indicated that the Ca ratings reflect its expectation of a high severity of loss related to these instruments in light of both banks' fragile financial condition, as well as the low level of support assumed to be forthcoming from their private shareholders as well as from the Uruguayan authorities. 

 Comercial's operations were suspended for 30 days by the Central Bank of Uruguay on August 5, 2002, the same day it lifted the bank holiday it had imposed on July 30th for the whole financial system. Comercial had been partially intervened in February as the Central Bank purchased a stake in the bank following a scandal involving its Argentine shareholders. It remains unclear whether Comercial's private shareholders will step in to cover all of the bank's fixed term deposit and debt obligations. 

 . 

 Montevideo had been intervened on June 21, 2002 by the Central Bank of Uruguay. The Central Bank suspended the bank's operations on July 30th and has indicated it might liquidate the bank. 

 The following ratings were affected: 

 Banco de Montevideo S.A.: 

 - Long-term foreign currency deposits downgraded to Ca from Caa1. 

 - Long-term foreign currency senior debt downgraded to Ca from Caa1. 

 Banco Comercial S.A.: 

 - Long-term foreign currency deposits downgraded to Ca from Caa1. 

 - Long-term foreign currency senior unsecured debt downgraded to Ca from Caa1. 

 - Long-term foreign currency subordinated debt downgraded to Ca from Caa1.

title: Uruguay banks solvent enough for crisis- Central Bank .
text:
MONTEVIDEO, Uruguay, July 17 (Reuters) - Uruguay's banking system is solvent enough to weather this year's capital flight triggered by Argentina's worst-ever crisis, Central Bank President Cesar Rodriguez Batlle said on Wednesday. 

 Banks lost almost 30 percent of deposits from January to May, leading to a 63.9 percent fall in Central Bank foreign reserves up to mid-July as depositors pulled their savings, fearing knock-on effects of Argentina's financial crisis. 

 "Uruguay has done a magnificent job because the financial system has maintained itself. The country has respected people's deposits, banks are complying with their obligations and have good solvency," Rodriguez Batlle told reporters. 

 Still, Uruguay's Central Bank earlier this week extended its intervention of the Uruguayan unit of Argentina's Banco Galicia , which was suspended at the end of February for liquidity problems, and Compania General de Negocios, a bank controlled by Argentina's Banco General de Negocios. 

 Tiny Uruguay's economy, dependent on agriculture, tourism and banking, has been deeply shaken in recent months by fears of a repeat at home of the economic crisis in Argentina, where a chaotic recession has put banks on the brink of collapse. 

 Despite a $1.5 billion aid increase approved last month by the International Monetary Fund, Uruguay has suffered from a drop in deposits, June's abrupt currency flotation and a wave of downgrades from credit rating agencies. 

 Rodriguez Batlle said Uruguay should recover investor confidence if the country, in recession since 1999, reduces its fiscal deficit and resumes economic growth. 

 Uruguay's fiscal deficit was equal to 4.2 percent of gross domestic product by the end of March, a level which must drop to 2.5 percent this year to receive IMF aid. GDP fell 10.1 percent in the first quarter.

title: MOODY'S DOWNGRADES BANK FINANCIAL STRENGTH RATING OF BANCO DE MONTEVIDEO.
text:
MOODY'S DOWNGRADES BANK FINANCIAL STRENGTH RATING OF BANCO DE MONTEVIDEO FOLLOWING CENTRAL BANK INTERVENTION - PLACES FOREIGN CURRENCY DEBT RATINGS OF BANCO COMERCIAL ON REVIEW FOR POSSIBLE DOWNGRADE. 

 Moody's Investors Service 

 Moody's Investors Service lowered the bank financial strength rating (BFSR) of Banco de Montevideo S.A. (Montevideo) to E, from E+, following its intervention by the Central Bank of Uruguay. 

 Moody's also placed on review for possible downgrade the Ba3 and B1 long term foreign currency senior and subordinated debt ratings of Banco Comercial S.A. (Comercial). 

 The Uruguayan Central Bank stated that it took control of Montevideo on Friday, June 21, 2002 to facilitate its recapitalization and to ensure that its obligations are met. The Central Bank said it would also recapitalize Banco Comercial, which had received an earlier capital infusion of $133 million in February from the Central Bank and its private shareholders after suffering a large deposit loss. 

 Both banks reopened today, Monday, June 24th, and continue to meet their obligations with depositors. 

 Moody's noted that Banco de Montevideo's financial condition has been steadily deteriorating since the beginning of the year. Banco de Montevideo has been hit by a systemwide outflow of deposits as a result of contagion from Argentina's banking crisis. 

 Montevideo's E bank financial strength rating indicates that the bank has very weak intrinsic financial strength and requires external capital support. Banco Comercial's bank financial strength rating was also confirmed at E. The BFSRs of both banks are stable.

title: UPDATE 3-Uruguay floats  currency  as Argentina problems weigh.
text:
MONTEVIDEO, Uruguay, June 20 (Reuters) - Uruguay floated its peso on Thursday, abruptly ending a decade-old currency band system as a deep recession at home deteriorated due to spreading economic woes in neighboring Argentina and Brazil. 

 Uruguay is seen by many investors as the front line in the wider battle of Latin American nations fighting to avoid contagion from Brazil's deteriorating economy and Argentina, which is churning through its worst financial crisis ever. 

 "The exchange rates of our two neighbors are heaping major uncertainty on us," Economy Minister Alberto Bension said. 

 The peso closed nearly 10 percent lower as surprised investors rushed to shield themselves from a deep slump that has sparked a run on banks and shaken agriculture-dependent Uruguay's long-celebrated status as a stable financial oasis. 

 Uruguay's international reserves have plummeted over 40 percent this year amid attempts to keep the peso trading within its former band. The Central Bank said there would be only limited intervention to prop up the new floating currency. 

 The International Monetary Fund, which has given financial aid to Uruguay in an effort to keep it from spiraling down with Argentina, said Uruguay was a "classic contagion case" and welcomed the nation's "bold" currency move, while the U.S. Treasury praised the float as a "strengthened" foreign exchange policy. 

 Lines were relatively short at exchange houses in the capital Montevideo as many confused people asked each other why the peso's value had suddenly plummeted. Some banks reportedly refused to sell dollars until the market stabilized. 

 Several Uruguayans said their deepest fear was a repeat at home of the problems across the muddy River Plate in major trade partner Argentina, where a botched devaluation in January has put the entire financial system on the brink of collapse. 

 "The problem here is that until Argentina gets its act together, Uruguay can't fix itself either," said Sebastian Batista, a banker, as he waited to buy dollars he needs to pay off a car loan in a country where many people hold debts in the U.S. currency. 

 SHIELDING FROM CONTAGION 

 Shortly after sundown, many people in the capital banged pots and pans from their balconies in a traditional form of peaceful protest against the government measure. 

 Aiming to shield the region from Argentina's collapse, the International Monetary Fund may increase aid to Uruguay by $1.5 billion on top of a $769 million loan approved in March. 

 But any dramatic fall in the currency worries investors, who fear it could hurt the country's ability to service its approximately $6.6 billion foreign debt. Uruguay has been battered by a loss of export competitiveness due to its neighbors' devaluations and a dive in consumer spending, leading GDP to drop 10 percent in the first quarter. 

 Exasperated Uruguayan President Jorge Batlle this month slammed Argentine politicians as a "band of thieves" when asked about Argentina's impact on his economy. He later blamed the outburst on the stress of dealing with his country's crisis. 

 In this country of 3 million people, 15 percent of the work force is unemployed. The economy has never fully recovered from Brazil's 1999 devaluation, and many now worry the free-float at home could spark inflation. 

 The free float decision comes six months after Argentina, Latin America's third-largest economy, devalued its own currency by cutting it loose from a rigid one-to-one exchange rate with the U.S. dollar amid an economic crisis. Argentina's peso has since tumbled over 70 percent. 

 "They want to obviously try to preserve their international reserves and not spend them on the defense of some arbitrary exchange rate band. So from that perspective, the decision will help them do that," said Marco Santamaria, sovereign strategist at Lehman Brothers in New York. 

 "(But) if the exchange rate were to depreciate substantively, Uruguay's debt burden would become more difficult to manage in peso terms," he added. 

 Troubles in Brazil, fueled by investor worries that turbulence ahead of October's presidential elections will make it difficult to manage the country's hefty $274 billion debt load, have also hit Uruguay. 

 Under Uruguay's currency band system, the central bank intervened in the market to keep the currency trading within a certain range. Uruguay's previous system of controlled devaluations had left its exports unable to keep pace with those of major trading partner Argentina amid its peso fall. 

 As well as the new IMF loan, Uruguay has recently also won $500 million in aid from the Inter-American Bank, and the World Bank has pledged to lend $400 million over two years. 

 Uruguay's sovereign bonds did not react immediately to the news. 

 Bond prices had plummeted as investors shied away from Uruguayan debt while the country has been paralyzed by strikes against tax hikes and austerity measures. 

 Uruguay's problems have been compounded by a string of downgrades from ratings agencies, which expressed concern that Argentina's financial mess had sent Uruguay's bank deposits and reserves tumbling. (additional reporting by Brian Winter and Patricia Avila).

title: Argentina says Uruguay approves Galicia bond plan.
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina, June 20 (Reuters) - Argentina's Central Bank said Thursday its Uruguayan counterpart had told local Banco de Galicia it would not oppose plan's by its Uruguayan unit to return frozen savings to depositors. 

 Banco Galicia Uruguay, controlled by Argentine financial holding company Grupo Financiero Galicia , proposed earlier this month returning deposits to Uruguayan savers in the form of negotiable bonds or term deposit certificates to help generate liquidity amid a cash crunch. 

 The bonds for savings plan is similar to the one being offered to savers in crisis-wracked Argentina, where billions of dollars were frozen in December amid the country's worst ever economic crisis. 

 Uruguay's Central Bank had earlier called the plan "unsatisfactory" and said the bonds needed to offer better guarantees for deposit holders. The decision reversal was announced after Uruguay freely floated its peso on Thursday citing financial woes in neighboring Argentina and Brazil. 

 Banco Galicia Uruguay's troubles were sparked by Argentina's huge financial crisis. Uruguay has seen plummeting bank deposits and international reserves in recent months in reaction to a deepening four-year recession in its South American trade partner. 

 Uruguay's banking, tourism and agriculture-based economy has been hit hard by the recession in Argentina, forcing the government to end its decade-old currency band system. 

 Uruguay's Central Bank suspended activity at Banco Galicia Uruguay for 90 days and extended its control over Uruguay's second-largest private bank for another two months in mid-May. 

Uruguay's Central Bank first intervened to help Banco Galicia Uruguay in February after it lost roughly a third of total deposits in December and January, the ripple effects of a run on deposits at the Argentine parent bank, which sent depositors clamoring to withdraw funds from the Uruguayan institution. 

 Last month, three major credit rating agencies downgraded the ratings of many Uruguayan banks with negative outlooks to reflect the government's own downgrade, resulting from dropping Central Bank reserves and the decline of the domestic currency.

 But consumer confidence in what was once considered a regional financial safe haven has been rocked by Galicia's liquidity crunch.

 Last month, three major credit rating agencies downgraded the ratings of many Uruguayan banks with negative outlooks to reflect the government's own downgrade, resulting from dropping Central Bank reserves and the decline of the domestic currency.

 Banco Galicia Uruguay has proposed returning seized dollar accounts with an initial reimbursement amounting to 3 percent of all the funds held by depositors, the bank spokesman said. 

 Deposits would then be paid back in nine annual interest-bearing installments either as negotiable bonds or transferable term deposit certificates, he added.

title: UPDATE 1-Uruguay reserves sink by nearly a quarter in Feb.
text:
(Adds details; Economy Minister's, analyst's comments; byline) 

 MONTEVIDEO, Uruguay, March 8 (Reuters) - Uruguay's net international reserves fell by nearly a quarter in February to $1.906 billion, the Central Bank said on Friday citing debt payments and a fall in deposits in the banking system. 

 The government also said the economic crisis in neighboring Argentina had contributed to the decline in reserves. 

 Reserves fell $605 million in February, bringing the fall for the first two months of the year to $1.05 billion. 

 The Central Bank said 50 percent of the drop in reserves was due to a $514 million decline in deposits at private banks and because its foreign debt payments had not been accompanied by new bond issues. 

 Reserves also fell as the government sold $100 million as it tried to prop up its peso in January, days before Argentina devalued its currency. 

 To compensate for the loss, the government plans to tap a contingent line of credit for $200 million from the International Monetary Fund that expires in March, said Economy Minister Alberto Bension. 

 "Uruguay will access the $200 million from the IMF in the coming days," Bension said. 

 Uruguay agreed a new economic program with the IMF that can be supported by a new standby loan which the Uruguayan government said would be worth at least $400 million. 

 Bension also said the government would issue debt on international markets to obtain dollars. 

 Uruguay's historically stable banking system suffered a steep drop in deposits in February as banks Banco Comercial, the country's largest private bank, and the local unit of Argentina's Banco de Galicia faced problems. 

 Banco Comercial is being investigated by the Uruguayan Central Bank due to a judicial probe in Argentina of alleged illegal capital flight following the introduction in December of banking restrictions in Argentina. 

 Concern over the probe led the bank's main shareholders - J.P. Morgan Chase , Credit Suisse First Boston and Dresdner Bank - to announce their support for the bank and a plan to inject $100 million in fresh capital to ensure that it could continue to operate. 

 The Central Bank intervened in Banco Galicia Uruguay in February due to liquidity problems caused by a steep drop in deposits. 

 The banks' problems shook the entire Uruguayan banking system, which has traditionally received a great deal of money from Argentine account holders who viewed it as a safe refuge for their cash. 

 Bension said the banking system had stabilized since the injection of capital into Banco Comercial. 

 Gabriel Oddone, an analyst at the Center for Economic Studies said the drop in reserves was a serious cause for concern. The drop "is an alert sign for the economy going into the future ... above all because of the problem of confidence it provoked in the banking system." 

 SYMPTOMS OF ARGENTINE CRISIS 

 Tiny Uruguay - whose coveted "investment grade" credit rating was revoked in January by Standard & Poor's as contagion from Argentina showed signs of increasing - sees its economy shrinking 1.5 percent in 2002 under the deal, the economy ministry said in a statement. 

 Argentina's crisis has sliced revenues in Uruguay's tourist industry and forced the government to accelerate its regular monthly currency devaluations and make sweeping budget cuts. 

 Uruguay's economy has never fully recovered from the 1999 currency devaluation of its other giant neighbor and chief trading partner Brazil, which made its regional exports uncompetitive. (Additional reporting by Patricia Avila).

title: UPDATE 3-Argentina woes spread to Uruguay via Banco Galicia.
text:
(Recasts lede; adds plan to return deposits, updates 

 stocks) 

 By Anahi Rama 

 MONTEVIDEO, Uruguay, Feb 13 (Reuters) - Argentina's financial woes on Wednesday spread to neighboring Uruguay, where the Central Bank closed the local unit of Argentina's largest private bank for 90 days after a run on deposits. 

 The Central Bank said it would intervene in Banco Galicia Uruguay SA - wholly controlled by Argentina's Banco Galicia y Buenos Aires SA - and force a total suspension of activity for 90 days after the bank lost roughly a third of its deposits so far this year. 

 Officials from Uruguay's second-largest private bank said they may gradually return deposits in quotas or fixed-term deposits to clients, the vast majority of whom are Argentines seeking refuge from a devastating banking crisis at home. 

 Analysts said the liquidity crunch resulted from a lack of confidence in Galicia due to problems at its banking operations in Argentina, where many deposits have been frozen since December to keep local banks from collapsing in the wake of a traumatic currency devaluation in early January. 

 As shares in the group that controls Galicia fell, economists said Uruguay's banking system - widely seen as an foreign financial haven for Argentines - was still very stable but did face some limited danger of capital flight. 

 "For now, this is a lack of confidence specifically in the name Galicia rather than a systematic problem that could extend to other deposits in Uruguay," said Hernan Fardi, an analyst for the Maxinver.com consultancy in Buenos Aires. 

 "But there is a latent fear among Argentine depositors who may now pass their other deposits in Uruguay to the United States, for example," Fardi said. "So in that sense it's fair to say Argentina is having some contagion effect in Uruguay." 

 PROBLEMS ONLY AT GALICIA? 

Central Bank officials said it would not force changes in Galicia Uruguay's management, but an auditor would be appointed to review the bank's finances. No financial assistance was expected to be provided, officials said. 

 The shares in Grupo Financiero Galicia, which controls Banco Galicia, shed 9 percent to 33.2 peso on the Buenos Aires Stock Exchange, as traders worried about the group's overall financial health, amid overall light gains. 

 A Galicia Uruguay source told Reuters on Tuesday that the run on deposits saw more than $300 million withdrawn in just five working days. Galicia Uruguay said in a statement it had deposits of $1.4 billion and a net worth of $231 million at the end of 2001. 

 The source also said GFG's banking operations in Argentina were "very strong" thanks to the partial freeze in place on deposits to halt a run there amid a recession now in its fourth year. Ratings agencies, however, say that most of Argentina's banks are insolvent. 

 Analysts said the liquidity problem may also result from transfers by Galicia Uruguay to its Argentine headquarters. 

 But Uruguayan officials played down fears Argentina's problems could further affect banks in the mostly agricultural country, one of the few in Latin American to enjoy "investment grade" status from ratings agencies. 

 "Banks are strong," said Ramon Diaz, former president of Uruguay's Central Bank. "This isn't going to even come close to spreading to the rest of the system." 

 Meanwhile, Banco Comercial, Uruguay's largest private bank, is under investigation by the Central Bank due to a separate judicial probe in Argentina of alleged illegal capital flight following the Argentine deposit freeze. 

 Concern over the investigation led its primary shareholders - J.P. Morgan Chase, Credit Suisse First Boston and Dresdner Bank - to announce their support for Banco Comercial last week. 

 (Additional reporting by Brian Winter in Buenos Aires).

title: UPDATE 1-Argentine stocks end at lows unseen since early 1999.
text:
BUENOS AIRES, Argentina, July 4 (Reuters) - Argentine shares edged down on Wednesday, sinking to their lowest levels since Brazil devalued its currency in 1999, in the wake of presidential resignation rumors on Tuesday, traders said. 

 In an interview with La Nacion newspaper, President Fernando de la Rua dismissed as "nonsense" talk that he was "overwhelmed" and about to quit as president of Argentina. 

 The center-left coalition leader said the rumors were spread by people "speculating against the country." 

 The benchmark MerVal dropped 0.80 percent to close at 385.96 points, near its lowest point since Brazil's steep devaluation in mid-January 1999. 

 The MerVal touched a low of 384.98 earlier in the session which was marked by anemic volume of $6.4 million. Decliners tripled advancers 18 to six while six issues were unchanged. 

 Frustration with the torpor that has afflicted Latin America's third-largest economy for the last three years is reaching new heights. 

 A member of De la Rua's own party, Chaco provincial Gov. Angel Rozas on Tuesday said the president was "overwhelmed" by the ongoing crisis, which fueled talk the 63-year-old leader, treated last month for arteriosclerosis, might step down. 

 "No one would seriously pull out of an investment based on rumors. I think yesterday's rumors were an expression of desire by investors for what they'd like to see done," said Leopoldo Olivario of Bacque brokerage. 

 The currencies of Brazil and Chile tumbled on Argentine woes and Uruguay's central bank intervened for the fourth consecutive business day to defend its battered money. 

 The currency of Argentina's top trade partner, Brazil's real , closed seven cents lower at 2.42 reais per U.S. dollar, a 2.85 percent depreciation from Tuesday's close and a level not seen since Brazil's central bank announced aggressive plans to prop up that money on June 21. 

 Argentina's country risk rating - the spread between Argentine bonds and safe-haven U.S. Treasuries - was up 17 basis points at 1,094 basis points. 

 "The market will continue to trend down as long as we have political noise which will lead to expectations the government will have to pay high interest rates at the next Letes (Treasury bill) auction," said Luis Corsiglia of Corsiglia y Cia. brokerage. 

 The next Letes T-bill auction is scheduled for July 10 when $500 million in 364-day T-bills and $350 million in 182-day T-bills will be sold. 

 Another factor that has unnerved foreign investors is an ongoing spat between opposition Peronist Party provincial governors who complain the central government owes them about $225 million in transfer funds for social and other programs. 

 De la Rua's government negotiated the deal last November in exchange for a commitment by the provinces to freeze their primary public spending at 2000 levels for five years. 

 The government Tuesday night failed to reach an accord with opposition Peronist Party provincial governors, who control most of Argentina's 23 provinces, on the disbursement of social program and other funds. 

 Argentine stocks and bonds have suffered most of the year amid concern over Argentina's ability to pay its $128 billion debt during an economic slump verging on three years. 

 Investors want to see positive numbers in economic indicators such as tax collection that show that pro-competition, pro-growth measures announced by Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo over the last three months are actually working to pull the Argentine economy out of its lull. 

 Investors have said that only with sustained growth will Argentina be able to meet its debt obligations. U.S. markets, meanwhile, were closed for the U.S. Independence Day holiday.
